name: room
text: Room opened — goal: creators: Build PACKAGES + enrich tabs + draft elements; every one labeled 'Created by EXCAVA' + tes

name: Forge
text: To kick off our project, I think we should start by building packages, as this will give us a solid foundation to work from and allow us to organize our content in a logical way. By doing this first, we'll be able to create a clear structure for our tabs and elements to follow, making it easier to enrich and draft them later on. The trade-off I'm accepting here is that we'll be delaying the drafting of elements, which may seem like a pressing task, but I believe that having a well-organized package system will ultimately save us time and effort in the long run. This approach will also ensure that our final product is cohesive and easy to navigate, which aligns with our quality-first principle.

name: Vet
text: Vet — the skeptic — leans in: "Starting with packages *first* assumes we already know the structure we need—but what if the content itself dictates the organization? A better move might be to draft a few tabs and elements first, then let the natural relationships guide the package design. To settle this, we should compare: (1) a quick mockup of how tabs/elements *might* flow, versus (2) a proposed package hierarchy. The clearer vision wins."

name: Forge
text:
I think we should start by drafting a few key elements, as this will allow us to get a feel for the actual content and how it relates to each other, which can then inform our package design. By doing this, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially having to reorganize our elements later if our initial package design doesn't fit, but I believe this is a worthwhile risk to take in order to ensure our packages are truly tailored to our content. This approach will give us a more organic and effective structure in the long run, rather than imposing a preconceived package design on our content. By taking this approach, we're putting quality first and allowing the content to dictate the organization, which aligns with our team's law of prioritizing quality and real, not display, requirements.

name: Vet
text: Vet — the skeptic — raises an eyebrow: "Drafting elements first risks building a fragile tower of assumptions—what if the content changes and forces a costly reshuffle later? A safer bet is to sketch *both* a rough tab structure *and* a lightweight package outline up front, then refine them together. That way, we test organization without overcommitting to either side. Settle it by agreeing to a 30-minute shared sketch session where we map out the top 3 tabs *and* their proposed packages side by side—no deeper work until we both nod."
